title: Clearview AI scraped billions of faces
hook: Photos you posted publicly became a face-search engine for police.
collected: More than 30 billion photos scraped from the public web, per the Dutch regulator.
howObtained: Automated scraping of websites and social media.
inferred: Face templates (biometric identifiers) that let a photo be matched to a person.
done: Clearview built a face-search tool sold mainly to law enforcement. EU regulators found it processed biometric data illegally.
label: DOCUMENTED
labelNote: Multiple regulator decisions. Clearview disputes EU jurisdiction.

companyResponse.text: Clearview says it does not serve EU customers and disputes that EU law applies; it did not object to the Dutch decision.

outcome.text: Fines in Italy, Greece, France (€20 million each) and the Netherlands (€30.5 million), largely unpaid. The UK fine is still in the courts. A US class settlement approved in March 2025 was vacated by the Seventh Circuit on 13 July 2026.

sources.title: Clearview AI hit with its largest GDPR fine yet
Seventh Circuit undoes novel privacy class settlement

limits: Fines exist on paper but are hard to collect across borders.
whyItMatters: Your face is a password you can't change.

title: Antivirus software sold users' browsing histories
hook: A privacy tool was itself the leak.
collected: Detailed web browsing data from Avast's antivirus and browser extensions.
howObtained: Software users installed to protect their privacy and security.
inferred: Interests, purchases, health, religion and more, from sites visited.
done: The FTC alleged Avast's subsidiary Jumpshot sold browsing data from 2014 to 2020 to more than 100 third parties.
label: DOCUMENTED
labelNote: FTC order. No admission of wrongdoing.

outcome.text: $16.5 million for consumer refunds and a ban on selling browsing data for advertising.

sources.title: FTC Order Will Ban Avast from Selling Browsing Data for Advertising Purposes

whyItMatters: Who watches the watchers? Sometimes nobody.

title: Delta's AI pricing: what it told investors versus senators
hook: 'AI pricing' can mean demand forecasting or personal targeting. Delta says it's the first.
collected: Demand and market data; Delta says no personal data is used in fares.
howObtained: Delta and its AI pricing partner Fetcherr.
done: Delta told investors it was expanding AI-assisted pricing (about 3% of its domestic network in mid-2025). After senators wrote to it, Delta stated that it does not and will not use individualised prices based on personal data.
label: STATEMENT
labelNote: Company statements. A widely quoted line about pricing 'to you, the individual' could not be verified by us.

companyResponse.text: "There is no fare product Delta has ever used, is testing or plans to use that targets customers with individualized prices based on personal data."

outcome.text: Senators said the reply left questions unanswered; no regulator action.

sources.title: Delta responds to misinformation around AI pricing

limits: We cannot see inside the pricing system either way.
whyItMatters: Watch the vocabulary: 'dynamic', 'personalised' and 'AI' pricing are different things.

title: Amazon's 'Project Nessie' pricing algorithm
hook: The FTC claims an algorithm predicted when rivals would follow Amazon's price rises.
inferred: Which price increases competitors would match.
done: In its antitrust case, the FTC alleges Amazon used 'Project Nessie' to raise prices where it predicted rivals would follow, earning over $1 billion in extra profit.
label: ALLEGED
labelNote: Allegation in an FTC antitrust complaint (heavily redacted).

companyResponse.text: Amazon said the FTC "grossly mischaracterizes" an old tool meant to stop unsustainably low prices that "didn't work as intended, so we scrapped it".
companyResponse.source: Amazon spokesperson Tim Doyle via NBC News

sources.title: Amazon used algorithm to raise prices, FTC alleges

whyItMatters: Algorithms can push prices up across a whole market, not just for one person.

title: RealPage's rent algorithm and pooled landlord data
hook: Landlords shared private rent data; software recommended rents.
collected: Landlords' non-public rent and occupancy data.
done: The Justice Department alleged the shared data and recommendations amounted to illegal coordination among landlords.
label: ALLEGED
labelNote: DOJ lawsuit with a proposed settlement (no admission); court approval pending when checked.

companyResponse.text: RealPage said it was pleased with the settlement.

outcome.text: Proposed settlement: no real-time non-public data, models trained only on data at least a year old, for seven years.

sources.title: DOJ's RealPage settlement: a blueprint for safer algorithmic pricing

whyItMatters: Pooling data through one algorithm can work like a cartel without anyone meeting.

title: Target's pregnancy prediction model
hook: The model is real. The famous story about an angry father is not confirmed.
collected: Shopping baskets (about 25 products, such as unscented lotion and supplements).
howObtained: Purchase history linked to a customer ID.
done: A Target statistician described a pregnancy-prediction model at a 2010 conference; the New York Times Magazine reported it in 2012 with an anecdote about a father learning of his daughter's pregnancy from coupons.
label: STATEMENT
labelNote: The model was described by a Target employee (STATEMENT). The father anecdote is single-sourced and was never confirmed by Target.

sources.title: Did Target really predict a teen's pregnancy? The inside story

limits: We could not open the NYT original.
whyItMatters: Inference from ordinary purchases is real. Not every viral story about it is.

title: Brown v. Google: tracking in 'Incognito' mode
hook: Users thought private mode was private. Google agreed to delete billions of records.
collected: Browsing data while users were in Incognito/private mode.
howObtained: Google analytics and advertising code on websites.
done: Plaintiffs alleged Google collected browsing data in private mode despite implying privacy. Internal emails quoted in court filings called Incognito 'effectively a lie'.
affected: A class of about 136 million users.
label: ALLEGED
labelNote: Private class-action settlement; no admission or finding.

companyResponse.text: Google called the suit meritless and said it never associates Incognito data with users.

outcome.text: Google agreed to delete billions of records, update disclosures and block third-party cookies in Incognito for five years. No cash for the class.

sources.title: Google will delete data collected in Incognito mode

whyItMatters: 'Private' mode hides your history from other people on your computer, not from websites.

title: Tax-filing websites sent financial details to Meta and Google
hook: Income, refund amounts and dependants' details flowed through tracking pixels.
collected: Filing status, income, refund amounts and details of dependants.
howObtained: Tracking pixels on H&R Block, TaxAct and TaxSlayer sites.
done: The Markup reported in 2022 that tax-preparation sites sent such data to Meta; a 2023 congressional report said the companies acknowledged sharing it.
label: DOCUMENTED
labelNote: Company acknowledgements in a congressional report; original findings REPORTED by The Markup.

companyResponse.text: TaxAct: "Protecting the rights and privacy of our customers is our top priority." Meta says it filters sensitive data; Google says site owners are responsible for what they send.

sources.title: Congressional report finds Meta and tax-prep companies recklessly shared taxpayers' data

limits: What Meta did with the data downstream is not documented.
whyItMatters: Pixels are everywhere, even on the most sensitive forms.
